headline: Type System Mechanics, Generics, Conditional Types, Type Narrowing & AST
description: Essential TypeScript interview questions covering advanced generics, mapped types, template literal types, conditional type inference (infer), branded types, covariance/contravariance, and compiler options.

questions.question: What is TypeScript, and what problems does it solve compared to plain JavaScript?
questions.answer: TypeScript is a statically-typed superset of JavaScript developed by Microsoft that compiles down to plain JavaScript. It adds optional static type annotations, interfaces, generics, and other tooling-friendly features on top of JavaScript's existing runtime semantics. It solves several problems that plain JavaScript has: (1) Type-related bugs (e.g., calling a method that doesn't exist on a value, passing a string where a number is expected) are caught at compile time instead of at runtime in production. (2) Large codebases become harder to refactor safely in plain JS because there's no static contract describing what shape an object or function argument should have - TypeScript's type checker catches broken call sites immediately after a refactor. (3) Editor tooling (autocomplete, inline documentation, 'go to definition', rename-symbol) is dramatically better with static types, since the IDE can reason about exact shapes of objects and function signatures. Because TypeScript is a superset, any valid JavaScript is (almost always) valid TypeScript, so adoption can be incremental. It's a purely compile-time/type-checking layer - the type annotations are erased during compilation, so it has no effect on runtime behavior or performance.

questions.question: What does it mean that TypeScript is a "superset" of JavaScript?
questions.answer: Being a 'superset' means every valid JavaScript program is (with very rare edge cases) also a valid TypeScript program - TypeScript doesn't remove or change JavaScript's runtime semantics, it only adds an optional static type system and a few syntax-level features (like type annotations, interfaces, and enums) on top. When you compile TypeScript, the compiler (tsc) performs type-checking and then strips out all the type-only syntax, emitting plain JavaScript that runs unmodified in any JS environment (browser, Node.js, etc.). This is why TypeScript can be adopted incrementally in an existing JavaScript codebase - you can rename a .js file to .ts and it will typically still compile, then you can progressively add type annotations. It also means TypeScript never introduces new runtime behavior or a different execution model; it's purely a development-time and build-time layer over JavaScript.

questions.question: What are the basic/primitive types available in TypeScript (boolean, number, string, array, tuple, enum, void, never, any)?
questions.answer: TypeScript's core primitives mirror JavaScript's runtime primitives, plus a few TypeScript-only type-system additions: 'string' - text values, corresponds to JS's typeof 'string'. 'number' - all numbers; JavaScript has no separate int/float, so there is only one numeric type (bigint is a separate primitive for arbitrary-precision integers). 'boolean' - true/false. Beyond these, TypeScript adds: 'any' - opts a value out of type checking entirely (assignable to and from anything); overusing it defeats the purpose of TypeScript. 'unknown' - the type-safe counterpart to any; you can assign anything to it, but you must narrow it before using it. 'void' - the return type of a function that returns no meaningful value (returns undefined). 'never' - represents values that never occur, e.g., the return type of a function that always throws or loops forever; it's also what's left when you've exhaustively narrowed a union down to nothing. Arrays are written as 'number[]' or 'Array<number>'. Tuples ('[string, number]') are fixed-length arrays where each position has a specific known type. Enums (e.g., 'enum Direction { Up, Down }') let you define a named set of constants - unlike most TypeScript constructs, enums actually generate runtime JavaScript code rather than being erased.

questions.question: What is type inference in TypeScript, and when does the compiler rely on it?
questions.answer: Type inference is TypeScript's ability to automatically determine the type of a value without an explicit type annotation, by looking at how the value is initialized or used. For example, 'let myName = "Alice"' is inferred as type 'string' without writing ': string'. The compiler relies on inference in several situations: (1) Variable initialization - the type of a variable is inferred from its initializer. (2) Function return types - inferred from the function's return statements, unless you explicitly annotate a return type. (3) 'Contextual typing' - when a function expression appears somewhere TypeScript already knows the expected shape (e.g., a callback passed to 'Array.prototype.forEach'), TypeScript infers the parameter types from that context, so you don't need to annotate the callback's parameters. (4) 'Best common type' inference - when inferring the type of an array literal with mixed-but-related element types, TypeScript looks for a type compatible with all the elements. The general guidance from the TypeScript team is to lean on inference rather than manually annotating everything, since it keeps code concise while explicit annotations are best reserved for function signatures (public APIs) where you want to lock in a contract or aid readability.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `any` and `unknown` types?
questions.answer: Both 'any' and 'unknown' can hold a value of any type, but they differ in how much safety TypeScript enforces afterward. With 'any', TypeScript disables type checking completely for that value - you can call methods on it, access arbitrary properties, assign it to/from anything, all without compiler errors, even if those operations would fail at runtime. With 'unknown', TypeScript still lets you assign any value to it, but before you can do anything with that value (call a method, access a property, pass it to a function expecting a specific type), you must first narrow it - using 'typeof', 'instanceof', a custom type guard, or a type assertion. This makes 'unknown' the 'type-safe' counterpart of 'any': it forces you to prove what the value actually is before using it, which prevents an entire class of runtime type errors that 'any' would silently allow. In practice: use 'unknown' for values coming from an untrusted or truly dynamic source (JSON.parse results, external API responses) and reserve 'any' for rare cases like gradually migrating JS code or working around a library with poor types - enabling the 'noImplicitAny' compiler flag catches accidental, unintentional 'any' usage.

questions.question: What are the `public`, `private`, and `protected` access modifiers in a TypeScript class?
questions.answer: These modifiers control the visibility of class members (properties and methods) at the type-checking level. 'public' is the default - a public member can be accessed from anywhere: inside the class, from subclasses, and from outside code that holds an instance of the class. 'private' restricts access to only within the declaring class itself - not even subclasses can access a private member. 'protected' is a middle ground: the member is accessible within the declaring class and any subclasses, but not from outside code that just holds an instance. Example: 'class Animal { public name: string; private id: number; protected age: number; }'. It's important to note these are purely compile-time constructs - TypeScript's access modifiers are erased when compiled to JavaScript and provide no runtime enforcement (unlike, say, Java's access modifiers). If you need genuine runtime privacy, TypeScript also supports native JavaScript private fields using the '#' syntax (e.g., '#id: number'), which are enforced by the JS engine itself, not just the type checker.

questions.question: What is an `enum`, and when would you use one over plain constants?
questions.answer: An enum lets you define a named set of related constant values, e.g., 'enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }'. Numeric enums (the default) auto-assign incrementing numbers starting at 0 unless you specify values; string enums require each member to be initialized with a string literal (e.g., 'enum Direction { Up = "UP", Down = "DOWN" }'). Enums are unusual among TypeScript features in that they are not purely erased at compile time - unlike interfaces or type aliases, TypeScript actually generates a real JavaScript object at runtime that you can inspect. You'd reach for an enum when you want a fixed, named set of related values with IDE autocomplete and the ability to reference the whole group by a common name - e.g., HTTP status categories, UI states, or command types. That said, many modern TypeScript codebases prefer a union of string literals (e.g., 'type Direction = "UP" | "DOWN"') or an 'as const' object over enums, because literal unions have no runtime footprint, avoid quirks like numeric enums' bidirectional (reverse) mapping, and interoperate more predictably with plain JavaScript and JSON.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `tsconfig.json`, and what are a few compiler options it commonly controls?
questions.answer: The presence of a 'tsconfig.json' file marks the root of a TypeScript project and specifies both the files the compiler should include and the compiler options used to check and emit them. When you run 'tsc' with no input files, the compiler walks up from the current directory looking for this file. Common options include: 'target' - which ECMAScript version to compile down to (e.g., 'ES2020'); 'module' - which module system to emit ('commonjs', 'ESNext', etc.); 'strict' - turns on the full family of strict type-checking flags (e.g., 'strictNullChecks', 'noImplicitAny'); 'outDir'/'rootDir' - where compiled output goes and where source files live; 'include'/'exclude' - glob patterns controlling which files are part of the compilation; 'lib' - which built-in type declaration libraries (DOM, ES features) are available; and 'esModuleInterop' - smooths over interoperability between CommonJS and ES module imports. You can also 'extend' a base config (e.g., a shared '@tsconfig/node18' package) to avoid duplicating boilerplate across multiple projects, and 'references' supports splitting a large codebase into multiple linked TypeScript projects (project references).

questions.question: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined` in TypeScript?
questions.answer: Both represent 'absence of a value' in JavaScript, and TypeScript gives each its own corresponding type. 'undefined' is the value a variable has when it's been declared but not assigned, and it's what a function returns implicitly if it has no return statement, or what you get accessing a missing object property or an out-of-bounds array index. 'null' is an explicit, intentional 'no value' that a developer assigns deliberately (e.g., 'let user: User | null = null' before a user is loaded). How TypeScript treats these depends entirely on the 'strictNullChecks' compiler flag. With it off, 'null' and 'undefined' are assignable to any type (similar to how languages without null-checking, like older Java, behave), which is a major historical source of 'cannot read property of undefined' bugs. With 'strictNullChecks' on (recommended, and part of 'strict' mode), 'null' and 'undefined' are only assignable to their own types and to 'unknown'/'any' - meaning if a variable's type is just 'string', you can't assign 'null' to it; you'd have to type it as 'string | null' and then explicitly narrow/check before use.

questions.question: How do you define optional parameters and default parameters in a TypeScript function?
questions.answer: An optional parameter is marked with a '?' after its name, e.g., 'function greet(name: string, greeting?: string) { ... }'. Its inferred type automatically becomes 'T | undefined', and optional parameters must come after all required parameters in the parameter list. Callers may omit it entirely. A default parameter is given an initializer, e.g., 'function greet(name: string, greeting: string = "Hello") { ... }'; if the caller omits the argument (or explicitly passes 'undefined'), the default value is used. A default parameter's type is inferred from the default value unless you annotate it explicitly, and - unlike optional parameters - a parameter with a default value can appear before required parameters and is still considered 'optional' from the caller's perspective (TypeScript treats it like an optional parameter for call-signature purposes). Both are compile-time-checked, but default parameters also inject actual runtime logic (an 'if undefined, use default' check) into the emitted JavaScript, whereas plain optional-parameter annotations affect only the type checking, not runtime behavior.

questions.question: What is the difference between an `interface` and a `type` alias, and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.answer: Both let you name an object shape and, for the most part, are interchangeable - an interface can be used almost anywhere a type alias's object shape can be. The core structural difference is extensibility: an interface can be 're-opened' - if you declare 'interface Window { title: string }' twice in your codebase, TypeScript automatically merges them into one interface with both sets of members ('declaration merging'). A type alias cannot do this; declaring 'type Window = {...}' twice with the same name is a compile error ('Duplicate identifier'). Related to this, type aliases (not interfaces) can name things other than object shapes - unions ('type ID = string | number'), primitives, tuples, mapped types, and conditional types. To 'extend' one type from another, interfaces use the 'extends' keyword; type aliases combine other types via intersection ('&'). There's also a subtle behavioral difference when combining conflicting members: extending two interfaces with an incompatible property is a straight compile error, whereas intersecting two conflicting types silently resolves the property to 'never' (since it must satisfy both types simultaneously). The TypeScript team's official guidance (and generally the community heuristic) is: default to 'interface' until you specifically need a feature only 'type' offers (unions, mapped/conditional types, etc.) - interfaces also tend to produce more readable error messages, and using 'extends' with interfaces can be more compiler-performant than repeated intersections in very large codebases.

questions.question: What are generics in TypeScript, and why are they useful? Write a simple generic function as an example.
questions.answer: Generics let you write a function, interface, or class that works across a range of types while still preserving type information, rather than either locking it to one specific type or giving up type safety entirely with 'any'. The classic example is an 'identity' function: 'function identity<Type>(arg: Type): Type { return arg; }'. Here 'Type' is a type variable - when you call 'identity("hello")', TypeScript infers 'Type' as 'string' and the return value is correctly typed as 'string', unlike a version typed with 'any' which would lose that information on the way out. Generics are useful because they let you build genuinely reusable components (think 'Array<T>', 'Promise<T>', or a custom 'Box<T>' container) whose internal logic doesn't depend on a specific type, while still giving consumers full type safety and IntelliSense for whatever type they instantiate it with. You can constrain a generic with 'extends' to require certain capabilities (e.g., 'function loggingIdentity<Type extends { length: number }>(arg: Type)' ensures 'arg' has a '.length' property), and you can give generic parameters defaults (e.g., '<T = string>'), similar to default function parameters.

questions.question: What is the difference between union types (`|`) and intersection types (`&`)?
questions.answer: A union type ('A | B') describes a value that could be any one of several types - 'string | number' means 'this value is either a string or a number'. Because TypeScript can't guarantee which member you're dealing with at any given point, it only allows operations that are valid across every member of the union unless you first narrow the type (e.g., you can't call '.toUpperCase()' on a 'string | number' without first checking 'typeof x === "string"'). An intersection type ('A & B') combines multiple types into one that must satisfy all of them simultaneously - a value typed 'Colorful & Circle' must have every member from both 'Colorful' and 'Circle'. Intersections are mainly used to compose object types together (mixing in multiple sets of properties), and are the type-alias equivalent of what 'interface ... extends' does. A useful mental model: union is 'or' (fewer guaranteed capabilities, since you only know what's common to all members), while intersection is 'and' (more guaranteed capabilities, since the result has everything from all the combined types). One gotcha: intersecting two types with conflicting property types (e.g., one says a property is 'string', the other says 'number') doesn't error - it collapses that property's type to 'never', since no value can satisfy both simultaneously.

questions.question: What is a discriminated (tagged) union, and how does it help TypeScript narrow types safely?
questions.answer: A discriminated union is a union of object types that all share a common property (the 'discriminant' or 'tag') where each member gives that property a different literal type. For example: 'interface Circle { kind: "circle"; radius: number } interface Square { kind: "square"; side: number } type Shape = Circle | Square;'. Because every member of the union has a 'kind' field with a distinct literal value, TypeScript can use a simple equality check or a 'switch' on 'shape.kind' to narrow 'shape' down to the exact member type inside each branch - e.g., inside 'if (shape.kind === "circle")', TypeScript knows 'shape' is specifically 'Circle' and lets you safely access '.radius'. This pattern is extremely common for modeling API responses, Redux/state-management actions, and any 'one of several known shapes' scenario, because it gives you compile-time guarantees rather than manual, error-prone property-existence checks. A major added benefit is exhaustiveness checking: in the 'default'/final 'else' branch of a fully-handled discriminated union, the remaining type is narrowed to 'never' - so if you assign that value to a variable typed 'never' (or pass it to a function expecting 'never'), the compiler will flag an error the moment you add a new member to the union but forget to handle it somewhere.

questions.question: What is "type narrowing," and what are the common ways to achieve it (`typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, equality checks)?
questions.answer: Narrowing is TypeScript's process of refining a broader type (usually a union) down to a more specific one based on the structure of your code - TypeScript follows the same control-flow analysis a human would, tracking what a value's type must be after a given check. Common narrowing techniques: 'typeof' checks - e.g., 'if (typeof id === "string")' narrows 'id' to 'string' in that branch, useful for distinguishing primitives. 'instanceof' checks - e.g., 'if (error instanceof TypeError)' narrows to the specific class, useful for class hierarchies and built-in error types. The 'in' operator - e.g., 'if ("radius" in shape)' narrows based on whether a property exists on the object, useful when union members don't share a common discriminant field. Equality/truthiness narrowing - comparing against 'null'/'undefined', a literal value, or simply checking truthiness (e.g., 'if (x)') narrows out falsy possibilities. Array.isArray() narrows a union like 'string[] | string' down to the array branch. You can also write a custom user-defined type guard (a function returning 'arg is Type') for narrowing logic that isn't expressible with a single built-in check, and discriminated unions (checking a shared literal 'kind'/'type' tag) are considered the most reliable narrowing pattern for complex object unions. Narrowing only lasts as long as TypeScript's control-flow analysis can 'see' it - reassigning a narrowed variable, or moving the check into a separate helper function without a type predicate, can lose the narrowing.

questions.question: What is a user-defined type guard (a function with an `x is Type` return signature), and how does it work?
questions.answer: A user-defined type guard is a function whose return type is a 'type predicate' of the form 'parameterName is Type', instead of a plain 'boolean'. Example: 'function isFish(pet: Fish | Bird): pet is Fish { return (pet as Fish).swim !== undefined; }'. The function body still just returns a normal boolean at runtime - the 'pet is Fish' annotation is a compile-time-only signal that tells TypeScript: 'whenever this function returns true, narrow the argument to Fish in the calling code's control flow.' So after 'if (isFish(pet)) { pet.swim(); }', TypeScript treats 'pet' as 'Fish' inside that branch without needing a repeated 'typeof'/'in' check. This is especially useful for encapsulating narrowing logic that's more complex than a single 'typeof'/'instanceof' check (e.g., validating the shape of an unknown value, or checking multiple properties) so the check can be reused across the codebase while keeping call sites clean. One important caveat: the compiler trusts the predicate you write - it doesn't verify that your implementation actually corresponds to the claimed type, so a poorly written or incorrect predicate can 'lie' to the type system and introduce unsound narrowing (a runtime bug the type checker won't catch).

questions.question: What are some of the built-in utility types (`Partial`, `Required`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`, `Readonly`), and when would you use each?
questions.answer: TypeScript ships a set of globally available generic utility types built from mapped and conditional types, useful for deriving new types from existing ones without repeating yourself: 'Partial<T>' makes every property of 'T' optional - handy for PATCH-style update functions where any subset of fields might be provided, e.g., 'function updateUser(id: string, updates: Partial<User>)'. 'Required<T>' is the opposite - makes every property mandatory, stripping any '?' modifiers; useful when you've received a partially-optional config type but want to guarantee all fields are filled in after applying defaults. 'Readonly<T>' marks every property as 'readonly', so reassignment is a compile error - useful for representing immutable data or preventing accidental mutation of shared/frozen objects. 'Pick<T, Keys>' constructs a new type containing only the specified subset of properties from 'T' - useful for exposing a narrow public view of a larger internal type (e.g., 'Pick<FullUser, "id" | "name">' for a public profile). 'Omit<T, Keys>' is the inverse of Pick - it keeps everything except the specified keys, e.g., 'Omit<User, "passwordHash">' to strip a sensitive field. 'Record<Keys, Type>' builds an object type whose keys are 'Keys' and whose values are all 'Type' - useful for dictionaries/lookup maps, e.g., 'Record<"home" | "about", PageInfo>'. Internally, most of these (Pick, Partial, Readonly, Omit) are implemented as simple mapped types over 'keyof T', so understanding mapped types explains how they work under the hood.

questions.question: What does `strictNullChecks` do, and how does enabling it change how `null` and `undefined` are handled?
questions.answer: 'strictNullChecks' is a compiler flag (bundled into the umbrella 'strict' option) that fundamentally changes how 'null' and 'undefined' participate in the type system. With it off, 'null' and 'undefined' are treated as valid values for every type - a variable declared as 'string' can silently be assigned 'null' with no compiler complaint, which mirrors how non-null-checked languages like older Java/C# behave and is a major historical source of 'Cannot read properties of undefined' runtime crashes. With 'strictNullChecks' on, 'null' and 'undefined' become their own distinct types that are only assignable to themselves (and to 'any'/'unknown', and to a union that explicitly includes them) - so to allow a value to possibly be absent, you must explicitly write 'string | null' or 'string | undefined' in the type. Then, before you can use methods/properties on that value, TypeScript forces you to narrow it first (an 'if' check, a non-null assertion '!', optional chaining '?.', etc.), or the compiler flags an error like "Object is possibly 'null'". This makes absence-of-value bugs visible at compile time rather than at runtime. The TypeScript team explicitly recommends enabling this flag for any codebase where it's practical, since it eliminates one of the most common categories of JavaScript bugs.

questions.question: What is the `as const` assertion, and how does it affect type inference (literal types vs. widened types)?
questions.answer: By default, when TypeScript infers the type of a mutable ('let'/'var') or object-literal value, it 'widens' it to the general type rather than the exact literal - e.g., a variable holding '"GET"' gets inferred as 'string' (not the literal type '"GET"'), because the compiler assumes it might be reassigned to a different string later. 'as const' overrides this widening: appending it to an expression (e.g., 'const req = { url: "...", method: "GET" } as const;') tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest possible literal types for every part of that expression instead. Concretely, this means: string/number/boolean values become their exact literal types instead of the general 'string'/'number'/'boolean'; object properties are all additionally marked 'readonly'; and array literals are inferred as 'readonly' tuples (fixed-length, fixed-position) instead of general mutable arrays. This is especially useful when you need a value to satisfy a literal-union type - e.g., a function expecting 'method: "GET" | "POST"' would reject a plain object literal's inferred 'method: string', but passing the same object built with 'as const' works because 'method' is now typed as the literal '"GET"'. It's also a common technique for deriving unions from arrays of values (e.g., 'const colors = ["red", "green"] as const; type Color = typeof colors[number];').

questions.question: What are declaration files (`.d.ts`), and why are they needed when consuming plain JavaScript libraries?
questions.answer: A declaration file (ending in '.d.ts') contains only type information - interfaces, type aliases, and function/class signatures - with no actual implementation code; it's purely a description of the shape of some existing JavaScript. Declaration files are needed because a huge portion of the JavaScript ecosystem (npm packages, browser/Node.js built-ins) is written in plain JS with no type annotations at all. Without a '.d.ts' file describing a library's API, TypeScript has no way to know what types a function's parameters or return values have, so it would either error on import or fall back to implicit 'any' everywhere, defeating type safety for anything that touches that library. Declaration files solve this by letting someone (often the library author, or the community via the 'DefinitelyTyped' repository, installed as '@types/package-name') describe the library's public API in TypeScript's type syntax, which the compiler reads alongside the plain JS code at compile time without affecting the emitted output. This is also how the browser DOM APIs and Node.js globals get their types - via bundled '.d.ts' lib files ('lib.dom.d.ts', '@types/node'). You can also hand-write your own ambient declaration file (using 'declare module' or 'declare function') for an untyped internal or third-party module your project depends on.

questions.question: How do abstract classes differ from interfaces in TypeScript, and when would you use one over the other?
questions.answer: An interface is a purely compile-time construct describing a shape - it's fully erased and produces zero runtime JavaScript. An abstract class (declared with the 'abstract' keyword) is a real class that participates in the actual class hierarchy at runtime: it can hold field initializers, implemented (concrete) methods with real logic shared by all subclasses, constructors, and access modifiers ('protected'/'private'), but it cannot be instantiated directly - 'new Shape()' on an abstract class is a compile error. It can also declare 'abstract' members (methods or accessors with no implementation) that every concrete subclass is required to implement, similar to how an interface's methods must all be implemented by a conforming object. Use an interface when you only need to describe a contract/shape - for function parameters, describing plain data objects, or when you want an object or class to satisfy multiple unrelated contracts (a class or object can implement many interfaces but can only extend one class, abstract or not). Use an abstract class when you want to share actual implementation code and state across a family of related subclasses, in addition to enforcing a contract - e.g., a base 'Repository' class with common CRUD logic and an abstract 'validate()' method each concrete repository must define. Both can technically enforce the same 'shape' contract; the deciding factor is usually whether you need shared runtime behavior.

questions.question: What is structural typing ("duck typing") in TypeScript, and how does it differ from nominal typing used in languages like Java or C#?
questions.answer: In a structurally typed system like TypeScript's, type compatibility is determined purely by the shape (members and their types) that a value has, not by what it was declared as or what name it was given. If a value has all the properties a target type requires, TypeScript considers it compatible - even if the value's declared type has a completely different name, or no declared type/interface at all. For example, a plain object literal '{ x: 100, y: 100 }' is assignable to a parameter typed 'interface Point { x: number; y: number }' with no explicit relationship between them; similarly, a class 'VirtualPoint' with matching 'x'/'y' fields satisfies 'Point' even though it never declares 'implements Point'. This is sometimes called 'duck typing' ('if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck...') applied at compile time. This contrasts with nominal typing, used by default in languages like Java or C#, where two types are only compatible if one explicitly declares that it implements/extends the other by name - an identical-looking class that doesn't explicitly implement an interface is not considered compatible, regardless of its shape. TypeScript chose structural typing because it mirrors how JavaScript objects already behave at runtime (duck-typed, prototype-based), but it does mean two unrelated types with the same shape are freely interchangeable, which is why patterns like branded/nominal types exist for the cases where you specifically want to simulate Java/C#-style nominal distinctions.

questions.question: What is the `keyof` operator, and how is it commonly used together with generics?
questions.answer: 'keyof' is a type operator that takes an object type and produces a union of its property names as string (or number/symbol) literal types. For example, given 'interface Person { name: string; age: number }', 'keyof Person' produces the type '"name" | "age"'. It's most commonly paired with generics to write functions that safely operate on 'some property of some object' without knowing either in advance. The canonical example is a type-safe 'getProperty' helper: 'function getProperty<Type, Key extends keyof Type>(obj: Type, key: Key) { return obj[key]; }'. Here, 'Key extends keyof Type' constrains the second generic parameter to only the actual property names that exist on 'Type', so calling 'getProperty(person, "age")' type-checks and correctly infers the return type as 'number', while calling it with a nonexistent key like '"height"' is a compile error. This pattern underlies many of TypeScript's built-in utility types - 'Pick<T, K extends keyof T>', 'Partial<T>', and 'Record<K, V>' are all implemented as mapped types iterating over a 'keyof'-derived union of keys. 'keyof' is also frequently combined with indexed access types ('Type[Key]') to look up the specific value type associated with a given key.

questions.question: How would you write a generic function that only accepts objects with a specific property, using a generic constraint (`extends`)?
questions.answer: You constrain a generic type parameter with 'extends' followed by an interface (or object type) describing the minimum shape required. For example, to write a function that logs an argument's length before returning it, you can't just write 'function loggingIdentity<Type>(arg: Type) { console.log(arg.length); return arg; }' - TypeScript rejects this because it can't guarantee an arbitrary 'Type' has a '.length' property. Instead: 'interface Lengthwise { length: number } function loggingIdentity<Type extends Lengthwise>(arg: Type): Type { console.log(arg.length); return arg; }'. Now 'Type' is constrained to any type that has at least a numeric 'length' property - strings, arrays, and custom objects with a 'length' field all satisfy the constraint, while a bare 'number' does not and produces a compile error at the call site ('loggingIdentity(3)' fails since 'number' has no '.length'). Critically, the function still returns the exact input type (not the widened 'Lengthwise'), preserving whatever more specific properties the caller's actual argument type had - so if you pass in '{ length: 10, value: 3 }', the return type retains the 'value' property too, unlike simply typing the parameter as 'Lengthwise' directly, which would discard extra properties from the return type.

questions.question: What are decorators in TypeScript, and what is a common use case for them (e.g., in Angular or NestJS)?
questions.answer: A decorator is a special declaration, written with an '@expression' syntax, that can be attached to a class, method, accessor, property, or parameter to observe, modify, or replace it via metaprogramming, without changing the original source. A decorator expression must evaluate to a function that's called at runtime with information about the thing it decorates (e.g., a class decorator receives the class's constructor). 'Decorator factories' - functions that return the actual decorator - let you parameterize the behavior, e.g., '@Component({ selector: "app-root" })'. When multiple decorators are stacked on one declaration, their factory expressions evaluate top-to-bottom, but the resulting decorator functions are invoked bottom-to-top (similar to composing functions). TypeScript's original decorator implementation is an experimental 'stage 2' proposal enabled via the 'experimentalDecorators' compiler flag (with 'emitDecoratorMetadata' additionally enabling runtime type metadata via the 'reflect-metadata' library); TypeScript 5.0 added support for the newer, standardized ECMAScript 'stage 3' decorators. The most common real-world use case is framework metaprogramming: Angular uses class decorators like '@Component' and '@Injectable' to attach configuration metadata that its dependency-injection and compilation system reads, and NestJS similarly uses decorators like '@Controller()', '@Get()', and '@Injectable()' to declaratively wire up routes, DI, and middleware - letting you describe 'what' a class or method does without imperative boilerplate registration code.

questions.question: What are conditional types in TypeScript, and how does the `infer` keyword work inside them?
questions.answer: A conditional type lets you express 'if/else' logic at the type level, in the form 'SomeType extends OtherType ? TrueType : FalseType' - if 'SomeType' is assignable to 'OtherType', the type resolves to 'TrueType'; otherwise it resolves to 'FalseType'. This becomes powerful when combined with generics, since the branch chosen can depend on whatever type a generic is instantiated with - e.g., 'type NameOrId<T extends number | string> = T extends number ? IdLabel : NameLabel;' picks a different result type depending on what 'T' actually is at each call site, letting you collapse what would otherwise require several function overloads into a single generic function. The 'infer' keyword, usable only inside the 'extends' clause of a conditional type, lets you declaratively capture (bind to a new type variable) a piece of the type being matched, rather than manually picking it apart with indexed access types. For example, 'type GetReturnType<Type> = Type extends (...args: never[]) => infer Return ? Return : never;' matches any function type and captures whatever its return type is into 'Return', which becomes the result if the match succeeds. This is exactly how the built-in 'ReturnType<T>' utility type is implemented. One subtlety: when inferring from an overloaded function type, TypeScript infers from the last (most general/catch-all) signature, not by resolving overloads based on argument types.

questions.question: How would you implement a `ReturnType<T>`-style utility type from scratch using conditional types and `infer`?
questions.answer: You write a generic conditional type constrained to function types, and use 'infer' inside the 'extends' clause to capture the return position: 'type MyReturnType<Type> = Type extends (...args: never[]) => infer Return ? Return : never;'. Walking through it: 'Type extends (...args: never[]) => infer Return' checks whether 'Type' matches the shape of 'some function' - using '...args: never[]' as the parameter type (rather than 'any[]') is a deliberate technique so the check works correctly against contravariant function parameter positions and doesn't leak an overly permissive 'any' into inference. If the match succeeds, 'infer Return' captures whatever type appears in that function's return position and binds it to the new type variable 'Return', which becomes the resulting type. If 'Type' isn't a function at all, the conditional falls through to the 'never' branch. Testing it: 'type Num = MyReturnType<() => number>' resolves to 'number'; 'type Str = MyReturnType<(x: string) => string>' resolves to 'string'. This is essentially the real implementation TypeScript ships as the built-in 'ReturnType<T>' utility type. The same pattern - extends a shape with an 'infer' placeholder in the position you want to extract - generalizes to writing your own 'Parameters<T>' (infer a tuple of parameter types), 'InstanceType<T>' (infer from a constructor's instance side), or 'Awaited<T>' (recursively infer through nested Promises).

questions.question: What are mapped types, and how would you use key remapping with the `as` clause (combined with template literal types) to derive new property names from an existing type?
questions.answer: A mapped type generates a new object type by iterating over a union of keys - typically obtained via 'keyof SomeType' - and producing a value type for each. The basic form is '{ [Property in keyof Type]: NewValueType }'; for example, 'type OptionsFlags<Type> = { [Property in keyof Type]: boolean }' takes any object type and turns every property's value type into 'boolean', while keeping the same property names. Mapped types also support 'mapping modifiers' - prefixing 'readonly' or '?' with '+'/'-' lets you add or strip those modifiers across every property (e.g., '-readonly [Property in keyof Type]: Type[Property]' strips 'readonly' from every property to build a mutable version of a type). Since TypeScript 4.1, an 'as' clause inside the mapped type's brackets lets you 're-map' each resulting key to a different name rather than keeping the original property name - this is 'key remapping'. Combined with template literal types, you can programmatically derive new property names from the originals: 'type Getters<Type> = { [Property in keyof Type as `get${Capitalize<string & Property>}`]: () => Type[Property] };'. Applied to 'interface Person { name: string; age: number }', this produces '{ getName: () => string; getAge: () => number }' - auto-generating a getter-method interface from a plain data interface. You can also filter out keys entirely by mapping them to 'never' in the 'as' clause via a conditional type (e.g., using 'Exclude' to drop a specific property name), and this same mechanism can even map over unions of object types keyed by a discriminant property, not just plain string/number/symbol keys.

questions.question: What is meant by covariance, contravariance, and bivariance in TypeScript's type system, and how does this affect function parameter type-checking?
questions.answer: These terms describe how the assignability relationship between two generic instantiations relates to the assignability relationship between their type arguments. Covariance: if 'Cat' is assignable to 'Animal', then 'Producer<Cat>' (something that 'make()'s a Cat) is assignable to 'Producer<Animal>' - the relationship direction matches, because anywhere you need something that produces an 'Animal', a thing that produces the more specific 'Cat' works fine. Return types and readonly/output positions are naturally covariant. Contravariance is the reverse: if you have 'Consumer<T>' (something whose 'consume' method accepts a 'T'), then 'Consumer<Animal>' is assignable to 'Consumer<Cat>' - a function capable of handling any 'Animal' can certainly handle the more specific 'Cat', so the direction flips relative to the type argument relationship. Function parameter positions are naturally contravariant under strict checking. TypeScript's structural type system automatically infers this variance for every generic type from its structure - you rarely need to declare it explicitly (though 'in'/'out'/'in out' variance annotations exist for rare edge cases involving circular types or as a performance optimization). This matters concretely for function type-checking: under the 'strictFunctionTypes' compiler flag (part of 'strict' mode), standalone function-type parameters are checked contravariantly, meaning a function expecting a narrower/more-specific parameter type generally cannot be assigned where a function expecting a wider parameter type is required. Notably, however, 'strictFunctionTypes' does not apply to method syntax (only to function-type properties/variables) - this is a deliberate, historically bivariant exception the TypeScript team kept for practical reasons (particularly around sound handling of common OOP patterns), which is a well-known source of confusion since a method-shorthand signature and an equivalent property typed as a function type can behave differently under the same assignment.

questions.question: What is "distributive" behavior in conditional types when applied to a union type, and when does it matter in practice?
questions.answer: When a conditional type's checked type is a 'naked' generic type parameter (not wrapped in anything, e.g., not inside an array or tuple) and you instantiate that parameter with a union, TypeScript automatically 'distributes' the conditional over each member of the union individually and unions the results back together, rather than evaluating the condition once against the whole union. For example: 'type ToArray<Type> = Type extends any ? Type[] : never;' - plugging in 'ToArray<string | number>' doesn't check '(string | number) extends any' once; instead it distributes as 'ToArray<string> | ToArray<number>', evaluating to 'string[] | number[]'. This distributive behavior is usually the desired outcome - it's how many built-in utility types (like 'Exclude<T, U>') work correctly across unions, filtering or transforming each member independently. But sometimes you specifically want the union treated as one single type rather than distributed member-by-member - for example, to check 'does this whole union extend some type' rather than 'does each member individually extend it'. To opt out of distribution, you wrap both sides of the 'extends' clause in a tuple/square brackets: 'type ToArrayNonDist<Type> = [Type] extends [any] ? Type[] : never;'. Now 'ToArrayNonDist<string | number>' evaluates the condition against the union as a single, non-distributed entity, producing '(string | number)[]' instead of 'string[] | number[]'. Understanding this distinction matters in practice whenever you're debugging why a custom conditional-type utility produces a union of results instead of a single result (or vice versa) - it's almost always because of accidental (or missing) distribution over a union type argument.

questions.question: How would you design a type-safe event emitter using generics and discriminated unions so that event names and their payload types stay in sync?
questions.answer: The standard pattern is to define an 'event map' type - an object type (or 'Record') whose keys are the event names and whose values are the corresponding payload types, then build a generic emitter class parameterized by that map. For example: 'type UserEvents = { userLoggedIn: { userId: string; timestamp: Date }; userLoggedOut: { userId: string } };' and then 'class TypedEventEmitter<TEvents extends Record<string, unknown>> { on<K extends keyof TEvents>(event: K, listener: (payload: TEvents[K]) => void): void { ... } emit<K extends keyof TEvents>(event: K, payload: TEvents[K]): void { ... } }'. The key technique is using a generic type parameter 'K extends keyof TEvents' on the methods themselves (rather than just typing the parameter as the union 'keyof TEvents' directly) - this lets TypeScript infer the specific event name from the call site and correlate it with the matching payload type via the indexed access 'TEvents[K]', rather than collapsing to the union of all possible payloads. With this setup, 'emitter.on("userLoggedIn", (payload) => { payload.userId })' gives 'payload' the exact 'userId'/'timestamp' shape with full autocomplete, while 'emitter.on("userLoggedIn", ...)' with a typo, or 'emitter.emit("userLoggedIn", { userId: "1" })' missing the required 'timestamp', both produce compile errors instead of silent runtime bugs. Discriminated unions become relevant when a single event's payload itself needs to represent one of several distinct shapes (e.g., success/error variants) - you'd give each variant a literal discriminant field so subscribers can safely narrow within the handler. One practical wrinkle when wrapping Node's built-in 'EventEmitter' class specifically: its 'on'/'emit' method signatures use '(...args: any[]) => void', which is wider than a strongly-typed '(...args: TEvents[K]) => void', and because function parameters are checked contravariantly under 'strictFunctionTypes', naively overriding those methods with narrower types can trigger a type error - commonly worked around by composing rather than extending 'EventEmitter', or by using an interface-merging/declaration-based override.

questions.question: What are branded (or "tagged") types, and what problem do they solve that a plain type alias cannot (e.g., distinguishing two structurally identical string types)?
questions.answer: Because TypeScript uses structural typing, a plain type alias like 'type UserId = string' offers zero extra safety at the type level - a 'UserId' and a 'ProductId' (also aliased from 'string') are completely interchangeable, since TypeScript only cares about shape, and both are just strings underneath. This means a function expecting a 'UserId' will happily accept any random string, including an accidentally-swapped 'ProductId' - the alias is purely documentation with no compiler enforcement. Branded types (also called 'nominal types' or 'opaque types') work around this by intersecting the base primitive with an object type containing a synthetic, non-existent 'brand'/'tag' property: 'type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly __brand: B }; type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">; type ProductId = Brand<string, "ProductId">;'. Now, even though both are structurally 'string plus a tag', the tag's literal value differs, so 'UserId' and 'ProductId' are no longer mutually assignable - passing a 'ProductId' where a 'UserId' is expected becomes a compile error. Since no real string value naturally has this fake '__brand' property, you can't produce a branded value by just writing a string literal; you typically create one via a type assertion ('"u123" as UserId') or, better, a 'smart constructor' function that validates the raw value at runtime before asserting the brand. It's crucial to understand that branding is a purely compile-time fiction: the '__brand' property doesn't exist at runtime, it's erased along with all other TypeScript-only syntax, so branded types can still be bypassed via type assertions and provide no runtime guarantee - they're a tool for catching logical mix-up bugs (like swapped IDs, or unvalidated vs. sanitized strings) at compile time, not a substitute for runtime validation.

questions.question: What is excess property checking, and why does TypeScript apply it to object literals assigned directly to a typed variable but not to a variable assigned via an intermediate reference?
questions.answer: Excess property checking is extra validation TypeScript performs specifically on 'fresh' object literals when they're assigned directly to a typed variable, passed directly as a function argument, or returned directly - it checks that the literal doesn't contain any property the target type doesn't declare. For example, given 'interface SquareConfig { color?: string; width?: number }', calling 'createSquare({ colour: "red", width: 100 })' (note the misspelled 'colour') is a compile error, even though structurally a '{ colour, width }' object would otherwise be assignable to 'SquareConfig' under normal structural-typing rules (since 'SquareConfig' has no required properties, and structural compatibility alone wouldn't flag an unrecognized extra property). TypeScript adds this stricter check specifically for object literals because typos like this are extremely common and almost always represent a real bug, whereas the looser general structural rule ('an object is compatible if it has at least the required properties, extra properties are fine') is useful for genuinely reusing broader objects. The check does not apply, however, when you first assign the literal to an intermediate variable and then pass that variable - e.g., 'let squareOptions = { colour: "red", width: 100 }; createSquare(squareOptions);' compiles without error, because 'squareOptions' is no longer a 'fresh' object literal at the call site; it's an already-typed variable, and ordinary structural assignability rules (which allow excess properties) apply instead - as long as it shares at least one common property with the target type (if it shares none, TypeScript still flags it as having 'no properties in common'). The recommended ways to legitimately allow extra properties are to add an index signature to the target type (e.g., '[propName: string]: unknown') if the type is genuinely meant to be open-ended, or use a type assertion ('as SquareConfig') to explicitly opt out of the check - though the TypeScript docs caution that most excess-property errors indicate a real bug rather than something to be worked around.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between using `enum`, a union of string literals, and an `as const` object for representing a fixed set of values in a large codebase?
questions.answer: 'enum' (e.g., 'enum Direction { Up, Down }') gives you a single named type you can reference for both the type and value positions, IDE autocomplete on the enum name, and - for numeric enums - a reverse mapping (looking up the member name from its value at runtime). But it comes with real costs: it's one of the few TypeScript constructs that generates actual runtime JavaScript (an object, plus special handling for numeric enums' reverse mapping), which adds to bundle size; numeric enum members default to plain incrementing numbers unless given explicit values, which is easy to misuse and doesn't serialize meaningfully to JSON/APIs; enums don't structurally match plain string/number literals from external sources (you often need explicit casting when a value comes from JSON or a database); and 'const enum' - a variant meant to fully inline values and avoid the runtime object - is restricted or entirely disallowed under 'isolatedModules' (required by most modern single-file transpilers like esbuild, SWC, and Babel) because those tools can't see across files to inline the enum's values, so this variant often can't be safely used in modern build pipelines. A union of string literals (e.g., 'type Direction = "UP" | "DOWN"') has zero runtime footprint (purely erased), serializes naturally as plain strings, and works seamlessly with JSON APIs and libraries with no special-casing - but it doesn't give you a single namespace to iterate over all possible values at runtime (you'd maintain a separate array/tuple alongside the type, and there's a common technique of deriving one from the other). An 'as const' object (e.g., 'const Direction = { Up: "UP", Down: "DOWN" } as const; type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction];') gets the best of both: a real runtime object you can iterate, dot-access, or pass around, whose values are inferred as literal types, while still compiling down to a plain object rather than special enum-specific runtime machinery, and it interoperates cleanly with plain strings. The general trend in modern, large TypeScript codebases (and reflected in current tooling guidance) is to prefer string literal unions or 'as const' objects over enums, reserving enums mainly for legacy code, existing conventions, or cases where the enum's own object identity is specifically desired.

questions.question: How would you diagnose and improve slow TypeScript compiler/type-checking performance in a large project or monorepo?
questions.answer: Diagnosis starts with TypeScript's built-in profiling flags: running 'tsc - extendedDiagnostics' surfaces high-level numbers (files checked, check time, memory used, instantiation counts), while 'tsc - generateTrace <dir>' produces a Chrome-DevTools-compatible trace you can load in the Performance panel to see exactly which types or files are the slowest to check. High 'Check time' generally points to expensive types (deep generics, large unions, heavy conditional/mapped type recursion) rather than raw file count, and high memory usage often points to overly complex or cyclic type relationships. Once you've identified the bottleneck, common fixes fall into a few categories: (1) Simplify expensive type patterns - the official TypeScript performance wiki specifically recommends preferring 'interface ... extends' over repeated intersection ('&') types for combining object shapes, since interfaces are checked as a single flattened type while type-intersection composition can require re-checking every constituent type on each comparison; preferring a common base type plus subtypes over one enormous union type for function parameters, since checking a large union against every use site is more expensive than checking a narrower base interface; and explicitly annotating function return types (especially on exported functions) rather than relying purely on inference, since TypeScript otherwise has to compute and cache the full inferred type at every call site. (2) Split the codebase using TypeScript's project references ('composite'/'references' in tsconfig), which breaks a large codebase into independently-buildable, incrementally-cached sub-projects so that changing one package doesn't force a full re-check of everything that (transitively) depends on it. (3) Tune tsconfig - narrow 'include'/'exclude' so unrelated files (tests, build artifacts) aren't part of the program; enable 'incremental' builds so 'tsc' reuses a '.tsbuildinfo' cache between runs; and enable 'skipLibCheck' to skip re-type-checking the internals of '.d.ts' files from 'node_modules', which is one of the most impactful, commonly recommended flags for cutting compile time on projects with many dependencies. (4) Keep TypeScript itself up to date, since the compiler team regularly ships targeted performance improvements to the checker across releases.

questions.question: What is the difference between an array type (`T[]`) and a tuple type in TypeScript?
questions.answer: An array type ('T[]' or 'Array<T>') describes a collection of unknown length where every element is the same type - e.g., 'number[]' can hold zero, one, or a million numbers, and TypeScript has no way to know the length ahead of time. A tuple type (e.g., '[string, number]') is a different, more specific construct: it's an array-like structure with a known, fixed length where each position has its own specific, potentially different type. So 'let pair: [string, number] = ["age", 30];' tells TypeScript that index 0 is always a string and index 1 is always a number, and trying to access an out-of-bounds index (like 'pair[2]') is a compile error, unlike a plain array where any numeric index is valid. Under the hood tuples are still just JavaScript arrays at runtime - TypeScript adds no runtime tuple type - but the type checker treats them specially, tracking a fixed 'length' literal type and per-position types. Tuples are commonly used to model things with a fixed shape, like coordinate pairs, or the return value of a function returning multiple distinct values (similar to Python's multiple-return-value pattern), e.g. 'function useState<T>(): [T, (val: T) => void]'.

questions.question: What does the `readonly` modifier do on a property, and how does `ReadonlyArray<T>` differ from a normal, mutable array?
questions.answer: Marking a property 'readonly' (e.g., 'interface Point { readonly x: number }') tells the compiler that, once the object is created, that property cannot be reassigned - attempting 'point.x = 5' is a compile-time error. Importantly, this doesn't make the property (or the object as a whole) deeply immutable at runtime; it's purely a compile-time check, and if the property itself holds an object, that nested object's own properties can still be mutated freely (e.g., 'home.resident.age++' is fine even if 'resident' is readonly, only 'home.resident = {...}' is blocked). 'ReadonlyArray<T>' (with the shorthand syntax 'readonly T[]') is the array equivalent: it exposes only the non-mutating methods of a normal array (like '.slice()', '.map()', indexing) and omits mutating ones like '.push()', '.pop()', or direct index assignment, all of which become compile errors. Unlike the 'readonly' property modifier (where a mutable and readonly-typed object with matching shape are assignable to each other bidirectionally via aliasing), assignability between 'Array<T>' and 'ReadonlyArray<T>' is one-directional - a mutable array can be assigned to a 'readonly' array parameter, but not vice versa, since that could let code retain a way to mutate something declared as readonly.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `void` and `never` return types for a function?
questions.answer: 'void' describes a function that completes normally but doesn't return a meaningful value - it's the type TypeScript infers for a function with no 'return' statement, or one that only has bare 'return;' statements; at runtime the function actually returns 'undefined', but 'void' signals 'the return value isn't meant to be used.' 'never' is fundamentally different: it describes a function that never successfully completes at all. This happens in two situations - a function that always throws an exception (e.g., 'function fail(): never { throw new Error(...) }'), or a function with an infinite loop and no break/return (e.g., a server's main event loop). Because a 'never'-returning function never actually produces control flow back to the caller, 'never' is also what remains when a discriminated union has been exhaustively narrowed down to nothing - which makes it a useful tool for writing 'assertNever' exhaustiveness-check helpers in switch statements: passing a value to a parameter typed 'never' only compiles if every possible case has genuinely been eliminated by preceding narrowing, so adding a new union member without handling it produces a compile error. A common mistake is treating them as interchangeable - a function typed 'void' is still expected to return control to its caller, just without a usable value, whereas 'never' asserts it will not.

questions.question: What are namespaces in TypeScript, and how do they differ from ES modules (`import`/`export`)?
questions.answer: A namespace (originally called an 'internal module', predating JavaScript's own module system) is a TypeScript-only construct that groups related code - interfaces, classes, functions, variables - under a single named object, accessed with dot notation (e.g., 'namespace Validation { export interface StringValidator {...} }' accessed as 'Validation.StringValidator'). Everything inside a namespace is private by default unless explicitly 'export'ed. ES modules, by contrast, are the standard JavaScript mechanism (native since ES2015) for splitting code across separate files, using 'import'/'export' statements, with each file forming its own scope and explicit dependency graph resolved by a module loader or bundler (webpack, esbuild, Node's own resolver, etc.). The key differences: namespaces exist purely to organize code within TypeScript's compilation and don't correspond to any native runtime module concept, so they can end up compiled into a single global object at runtime unless carefully split across files with reference comments; ES modules give you real per-file isolation, better tooling support for tree-shaking/bundling, and work identically to how modern JavaScript already works outside TypeScript. Because ES modules are now a native, standardized part of the language and integrate far better with the rest of the JavaScript ecosystem, the TypeScript team and most modern style guides explicitly recommend using modules over namespaces in new code - namespaces today mainly still show up in older codebases, in declaration files describing legacy global libraries, or occasionally for purely internal type-organization within a single file (not exported at the top level).

questions.question: What does the `declare` keyword do, and when would you use an ambient declaration?
questions.answer: 'declare' tells the TypeScript compiler 'trust me, this thing exists at runtime somewhere else - just check the types, don't emit any JavaScript for this declaration.' It's used to describe values, functions, classes, modules, or global variables that are implemented elsewhere (a script loaded via a '<script>' tag, a global provided by the runtime environment, a library with no bundled types) so the compiler can type-check code that references them without erroring on an 'undefined name' and without generating any actual initialization code of its own. This is called an 'ambient declaration' - it only exists in the type system, is fully erased at compile time, and produces zero runtime output. Common examples: 'declare const process: { env: Record<string, string> };' to describe a global injected by a bundler; 'declare module "some-untyped-package";' to tell TypeScript a module exists (typed as 'any') when no '@types' package is available; or 'declare global { interface Window { myGlobal: string } }' to add a property to the global 'Window' interface. Ambient declarations are typically placed in '.d.ts' declaration files, which by convention contain no implementation code at all - only type descriptions.

questions.question: What does the umbrella `strict` flag in `tsconfig.json` do, and which family of individual compiler checks does it enable?
questions.answer: 'strict' is a single 'tsconfig.json' compiler option that acts as a shortcut for turning on TypeScript's full family of stricter type-checking flags all at once, rather than having to enable each one individually. Setting '"strict": true' enables (among others): 'strictNullChecks' (null/undefined are only assignable to their own types unless explicitly included in a union), 'noImplicitAny' (errors on any value whose type the compiler can't infer and would otherwise silently fall back to 'any'), 'strictFunctionTypes' (more sound contravariant checking of function parameter types), 'strictPropertyInitialization' (class properties must be initialized in the constructor or have a definite-assignment/optional marker), 'strictBindCallApply', 'noImplicitThis', 'useUnknownInCatchVariables' (catch-clause variables default to 'unknown' instead of 'any'), and 'alwaysStrict' (emits 'use strict' and parses in strict mode). Individual flags within the family can still be selectively turned back off in the same config even with 'strict: true', by explicitly setting that one flag to 'false' - this is a common pattern when incrementally migrating a JavaScript codebase, where you want most strict checks on but need to temporarily relax one that's producing too many errors to fix immediately. The TypeScript team strongly recommends enabling 'strict' for any new project, since disabling it (or never turning it on) allows a large class of null/undefined and implicit-any bugs to slip past the type checker entirely.

questions.question: What is a getter/setter (accessor) in a TypeScript class, and how do you define one?
questions.answer: Getters and setters (collectively called 'accessors') let you define a class member that looks like a plain property to callers but is actually backed by a function, giving you a place to run custom logic - validation, computed values, logging - whenever the property is read or written. You define a getter with the 'get' keyword followed by a method-like body that returns a value, and a setter with the 'set' keyword followed by a method that takes exactly one parameter (the new value) and returns nothing. For example: 'class Person { private _name: string; get name(): string { return this._name; } set name(value: string) { if (value.length === 0) throw new Error("Name cannot be empty"); this._name = value; } }'. Callers interact with 'person.name' and 'person.name = "Alice"' exactly as if 'name' were a plain field - they don't call it like a method with parentheses - while the class retains full control over what happens on read and write (e.g., trimming, validation, or deriving the value from other private fields). A common pattern is pairing a private backing field (often prefixed with an underscore) with a public getter/setter pair to enforce invariants. Accessors require targeting ES5 or later when compiling down (since ES3 has no native getter/setter syntax), and you can define a getter without a matching setter to create an effectively read-only computed property.

questions.question: What are `@types` packages (e.g., `@types/node`), and how do they provide type information for plain JavaScript libraries?
questions.answer: '@types' packages are npm packages, published under the '@types' scope, that contain only TypeScript declaration files ('.d.ts') describing the public API of a JavaScript library that either doesn't ship its own types or is written entirely in plain JS with no type information at all. Most of them are sourced from 'DefinitelyTyped', a large, community-maintained GitHub repository where volunteers write and maintain type declarations for thousands of popular JS packages (e.g., installing 'npm install - save-dev @types/node' gives you types for Node.js's built-in modules, or '@types/lodash' for the Lodash utility library). When you 'import' from a package, TypeScript's module resolution automatically checks 'node_modules/@types/<package-name>' (in addition to the package's own bundled types, if any) to find matching declarations, so once installed, you get full autocomplete and type-checking for that library with no additional configuration in most setups. It's worth noting that many modern libraries now ship their own types directly (declared via a 'types' or 'typings' field in their 'package.json', pointing at a bundled '.d.ts' file), which is preferred going forward since it keeps the types in sync with the actual implementation - '@types' packages exist specifically to cover libraries that don't do this themselves, and can become outdated or mismatched with the underlying library's version if not actively maintained.

questions.question: What is a labeled tuple element, and why would you use one instead of a plain, unlabeled tuple?
questions.answer: A labeled tuple element (introduced in TypeScript 4.0) lets you attach a descriptive name to each position in a tuple type purely for documentation and tooling purposes, without changing the tuple's actual runtime behavior. Instead of writing 'type Range = [number, number]', which gives no indication of what each number represents, you can write 'type Range = [start: number, end: number]'. The labels show up in editor tooltips, autocomplete, and error messages, making the tuple's intent much clearer at a glance - especially valuable for tuples used as rest/spread parameter lists, where the labels effectively double as descriptive parameter names (e.g., 'function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(...args: [obj: T, key: K])' reads almost like a normal named-parameter function signature). Labels are purely cosmetic/type-level - they don't create actual named properties you can destructure by name (you still access elements positionally, e.g., 'range[0]'), and a labeled tuple type is still structurally compatible with an equivalent unlabeled one. The main reason to reach for them over a plain tuple is readability in public APIs or complex function signatures, where a bare '[string, number, boolean]' gives no clue what each value means, versus '[name: string, age: number, isActive: boolean]', which is self-documenting.

questions.question: What is the constructor parameter property shorthand (e.g., `constructor(private name: string)`), and what does it save you from writing?
questions.answer: Normally, defining a class property that's set from a constructor argument requires three separate pieces: declaring the property on the class, declaring the constructor parameter, and manually assigning the parameter to the property inside the constructor body (e.g., 'class Person { name: string; constructor(name: string) { this.name = name; } }'). TypeScript's 'parameter properties' shorthand collapses all three into one, by adding an access modifier ('public', 'private', 'protected', or 'readonly') directly in front of a constructor parameter: 'class Person { constructor(private name: string) {} }'. When TypeScript sees an access modifier on a constructor parameter, it automatically declares a class property with that name and visibility, and automatically assigns the incoming argument to it at the start of the constructor - no explicit 'this.name = name' line needed. This is purely a syntax convenience (it compiles down to the same 'this.x = x' assignment under the hood) but significantly reduces boilerplate in classes with many constructor-initialized fields, which is why it's extremely common in codebases using dependency injection (e.g., NestJS services frequently look like 'constructor(private readonly userService: UserService) {}'). You can freely mix parameter properties with regular constructor parameters that aren't turned into class members.

questions.question: What is the non-null assertion operator (`!`), and what risk does it introduce compared to a proper null/undefined check?
questions.answer: The non-null assertion operator is a postfix '!' you can place after any expression to tell the compiler 'trust me, this value is not 'null' or 'undefined' here,' removing those types from the expression's type without performing any actual runtime check. For example, given 'function liveDangerously(x?: number | null) { console.log(x!.toFixed()); }', the '!' silences the compiler's 'Object is possibly null or undefined' error and lets you call '.toFixed()' directly. Like all type assertions, it's a compile-time-only construct - it's stripped out entirely when compiled to JavaScript and has zero effect on runtime behavior. This is exactly the risk: if your assumption is wrong and the value actually is 'null' or 'undefined' at that point, there's no compiler safety net catching it - the code will throw a runtime 'Cannot read properties of undefined/null' error at that exact line, which is precisely the class of bug 'strictNullChecks' exists to prevent in the first place. Using '!' effectively opts back out of that protection for that one expression. It should be reserved for cases where you have information the compiler genuinely can't infer (e.g., you've already checked the value in a way TypeScript's control-flow analysis doesn't track, such as inside a callback, or you know a DOM element with a specific ID definitely exists on the page) - and even then, an explicit runtime check ('if (x != null)') or a proper narrowing pattern is generally safer and more self-documenting than silently asserting away the possibility of absence.

questions.question: What is the difference between a type assertion (`as Type`) and a definite assignment assertion (`!` placed after a variable or property name)?
questions.answer: Both use assertion syntax to tell the compiler something it can't verify itself, but they solve different problems. A type assertion ('value as Type', or the older angle-bracket '<Type>value' syntax) reinterprets the type of an existing expression's value - e.g., 'const canvas = document.getElementById("main") as HTMLCanvasElement;' tells TypeScript 'treat this as a more (or less) specific type than what was inferred,' and TypeScript only allows the assertion if the two types 'sufficiently overlap' (you can't assert a 'string' directly to a 'number' without first going through 'unknown'/'any'). A definite assignment assertion is a completely different mechanism, using '!' immediately after a variable or class property's name (not after an expression) at its declaration site, to tell the compiler 'this will definitely be assigned a value before it's used, even though you (the compiler) can't prove it through normal control-flow analysis.' The classic use case is a class property that's initialized in a separate lifecycle method rather than the constructor - e.g., 'class Component { data!: ResponseData; async init() { this.data = await fetchData(); } }' - where without the '!', 'strictPropertyInitialization' would otherwise flag 'data' as possibly used before being assigned. Another common case is a top-level variable assigned inside a function that TypeScript can't statically prove always runs, like 'let value: string; setup(); function setup() { value = "x"; } console.log(value!);'. In short: 'as Type' changes what type an expression is treated as; definite assignment '!' changes whether the compiler requires proof of initialization before use - neither one performs a runtime check, so both carry the same risk of masking a genuine bug if the underlying assumption turns out to be false.

questions.question: What is the `satisfies` operator introduced in TypeScript 4.9, and how does it differ from a type annotation or an `as` assertion?
questions.answer: 'satisfies' checks that an expression is compatible with a given type, without changing the type TypeScript infers for that expression the way a type annotation or 'as' assertion would. This solves a long-standing tension: writing 'const palette: Record<Colors, string | RGB> = {...}' with an explicit annotation validates the object's shape, but then every property gets widened to the annotation's type ('string | RGB' for every key), losing the more specific inferred type of each individual property (e.g., you lose the fact that 'palette.red' is specifically a tuple, not just 'string | RGB', so array methods on it become type errors). Writing 'const palette = {...} as Record<Colors, string | RGB>' avoids that widening but is unsound in the opposite direction - an 'as' assertion doesn't actually validate the object against the target type at all (assertions can lie), so an incorrect property name or misspelled key wouldn't be caught. 'satisfies' gives you both: 'const palette = { red: [255,0,0], green: "#00ff00", bleu: [0,0,255] } satisfies Record<Colors, string | RGB>;' flags the 'bleu' typo as an error just like the annotation would, while 'palette' itself keeps its precise, narrow inferred type afterward, so 'palette.red.at(0)' and 'palette.green.toUpperCase()' both still type-check correctly based on each property's actual literal type. It's especially useful for configuration objects, route maps, and any 'this object must conform to X, but I still want the most specific type possible for its individual values' scenario.

questions.question: How do you implement function overloading in TypeScript, and why must every overload signature be compatible with a single implementation signature?
questions.answer: Function overloading lets a single function name accept different combinations of parameter types and return correspondingly different types, by writing several 'overload signatures' (declarations with no body) immediately followed by one 'implementation signature' that actually contains the function body. For example: 'function createLabel(id: number): IdLabel; function createLabel(name: string): NameLabel; function createLabel(nameOrId: string | number): IdLabel | NameLabel { throw "unimplemented"; }'. Callers only ever see the overload signatures - calling 'createLabel(5)' resolves to the first overload and is typed as returning 'IdLabel', while 'createLabel("x")' resolves to the second and returns 'NameLabel'; the broader implementation signature itself is invisible to call sites, it merely has to be able to handle every combination of arguments the overloads promise to accept. This is why the implementation signature must be compatible with (a superset of) every overload signature - it's the only signature that actually runs, so its parameter types must be general enough to accept anything any overload claims to accept, and its return type must cover every possible overload return type. Order matters too: TypeScript picks the first overload that matches a given call, so overloads should be ordered from most specific to most general, or a more general earlier overload can silently 'shadow' a more specific one placed after it. In many cases, a single generic function or a well-designed union-type parameter can achieve the same result more simply than overloads - overloading is best reserved for cases where the relationship between input and output types can't be cleanly expressed with a conditional type or union alone (e.g., wildly different return shapes based on argument type).
