questions.question: What are indexed access types (e.g., `Person["name"]`), and how are they used to pull a property's type out of another type?
questions.answer: An indexed access type uses the 'Type["key"]' syntax to look up and extract the type of a specific property from another type - much like accessing a property on an object value at runtime, but operating entirely at the type level. For example, given 'interface Person { name: string; age: number }', 'type Age = Person["age"]' resolves to just 'number'. The key inside the brackets can itself be a type, including a union of string literals (to get a union of several property types at once) or a full 'keyof Type' expression to get a union of every property's value type. This is heavily used in generic, reusable type utilities - for instance, a generic 'Flatten<T>' type that extracts an array's element type can use 'T extends any[] ? T[number] : T', where 'T[number]' is an indexed access using the 'number' index type to pull out whatever type sits at any numeric index of the array. It's also the mechanism underlying many built-in utility types: 'Pick<T, K extends keyof T>' effectively uses 'T[K]' internally (via a mapped type) to look up the value type for each selected key. A key subtlety: you can only index with a key that's actually valid for the type - 'Person["height"]' would be a compile error since 'height' doesn't exist on 'Person', which is exactly the safety indexed access types provide over manually re-declaring a property's type by hand (which risks drifting out of sync if the source type changes).

questions.question: What do the `Exclude<T, U>`, `Extract<T, U>`, and `NonNullable<T>` utility types do, and how do they differ from one another?
questions.answer: All three are built-in generic utility types that filter a union type, but in different directions. 'Exclude<T, U>' removes from union 'T' every member that is assignable to 'U', keeping everything else - e.g., 'Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "a">' produces '"b" | "c"'. 'Extract<T, U>' does the opposite: it keeps only the members of 'T' that are assignable to 'U', discarding the rest - e.g., 'Extract<"a" | "b" | "c", "a" | "c">' produces '"a" | "c"'. 'NonNullable<T>' is a specialized, common case of 'Exclude': it strips 'null' and 'undefined' out of a type, so 'NonNullable<string | null | undefined>' resolves to just 'string' - functionally equivalent to writing 'Exclude<T, null | undefined>' but expressing the intent more directly. Internally, all three are implemented as conditional types distributing over the union: 'Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T' and 'Extract<T, U> = T extends U ? T : never' - the distributive behavior of conditional types over unions is exactly what lets these operate member-by-member rather than on the union as a whole. Practically, 'Exclude' and 'NonNullable' are common when narrowing an error/success union down to just the error cases (or stripping absence from an optional value's type before further processing), while 'Extract' is useful for pulling a specific subset of variants out of a larger discriminated union, e.g., 'Extract<Shape, { kind: "circle" }>' to get just the circle variant's type.

questions.question: How would you define a recursive type in TypeScript, such as one representing a tree structure or a nested JSON value?
questions.answer: A recursive type is a type alias or interface that references itself in its own definition, which TypeScript supports as long as the self-reference is nested inside an object, array, tuple, or union rather than appearing as a direct top-level alias (a bare 'type X = X' is rejected as circular). A simple tree node: 'type TreeNode<T> = { value: T; children: TreeNode<T>[] };' - here 'children' is an array of the same 'TreeNode<T>' type, letting the structure nest to arbitrary depth. A classic, slightly trickier example is modeling valid JSON: 'type JSONValue = string | number | boolean | null | JSONValue[] | { [key: string]: JSONValue };' - this correctly rejects values that aren't valid JSON (like a class instance or a function) while accepting arbitrarily deep nested objects/arrays, something a simple 'Record<string, any>' can't enforce (with 'any', you could sneak a non-JSON-serializable value like an 'Error' instance right through the type checker). Interfaces can also reference themselves recursively and, unlike some historical restrictions on deeply-recursive type aliases, interfaces have always supported this cleanly since they're resolved lazily. When writing functions that operate on a recursive type (e.g., traversing a tree), the function itself is typically also recursive, calling itself on each child node - the type definition and the runtime traversal logic mirror each other's recursive structure.

questions.question: What is the difference between shallow and deep immutability in TypeScript, and how would you write a `DeepReadonly<T>` mapped type?
questions.answer: The built-in 'Readonly<T>' utility type (and the 'readonly' modifier in general) only provides shallow immutability: it prevents reassigning the top-level properties of an object, but if any of those properties is itself an object or array, that nested value's own properties remain fully mutable - 'readonlyPerson.address.city = "..."' would still be allowed even if 'readonlyPerson' itself is 'Readonly<Person>', because only the outer 'address' property (the reference) is protected, not what it points to. Deep immutability means every level of nesting is locked down, all the way down to primitive leaf values. You get this by writing a recursive mapped type that checks, for every property, whether its value type is itself an object - if so, it recurses into 'DeepReadonly' again; if not (a primitive, function, etc.), it stops and leaves the type as-is: 'type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? readonly DeepReadonly<U>[] : T extends object ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> } : T;' (a special-case branch for arrays is typically added first, since mapping over an array's index signature directly doesn't produce a proper readonly-tuple/array type). Applying 'DeepReadonly<Person>' to a type with a nested 'address' object now makes 'person.address.city = "..."' a compile error too, since 'address' itself resolves to a further 'DeepReadonly<Address>' type rather than a plain mutable 'Address'. As with all 'readonly' typing in TypeScript, this is purely a compile-time guarantee - there's no runtime enforcement (unlike 'Object.freeze()', which does provide actual runtime immutability, though only shallowly unless applied recursively at every level too).

questions.question: How would you use module augmentation to add a custom property (e.g., `req.user`) to an existing library's type, such as Express's `Request` interface?
questions.answer: Module augmentation lets you extend the types of an existing module you don't own (like a third-party library) by re-opening one of its declared interfaces and adding new members, relying on TypeScript's declaration-merging behavior for interfaces. For Express specifically, the actual 'Request' interface lives in the 'express-serve-static-core' package (which '@types/express' re-exports), so you write a '.d.ts' file that imports/references that module and re-declares the interface with your additions: 'declare module "express-serve-static-core" { interface Request { user?: { id: string; email: string }; } }'. Because TypeScript merges same-named interface declarations within the same module scope, this doesn't replace Express's original 'Request' interface - it adds 'user' as an additional optional property alongside everything Express already defines, so every 'Request' object throughout your codebase (in route handlers, middleware, etc.) is now typed as having an optional 'user' field, without needing to import a custom type or cast anything. An older, still-commonly-seen alternative pattern augments the ambient global 'Express' namespace instead ('declare global { namespace Express { interface Request { user?: ... } } }'), which achieves a similar result but is considered slightly outdated in favor of directly augmenting 'express-serve-static-core'. A common real-world use is an authentication middleware that attaches the decoded user to the request (e.g., 'req.user = decodedToken; next();') - without the augmentation, TypeScript would reject that assignment since 'user' isn't part of Express's built-in 'Request' type.

questions.question: What is declaration merging in TypeScript, and how does it apply when the same `interface` is declared more than once?
questions.answer: Declaration merging is a TypeScript compiler behavior where two or more separate declarations sharing the same name are automatically combined into a single definition, rather than the second declaration causing a 'duplicate identifier' error or silently overwriting the first. Interfaces are the most common case: if you declare 'interface User { id: number; name: string }' and, elsewhere (even in a different file), declare 'interface User { email: string }' again, TypeScript merges them into one effective interface with all four properties ('id', 'name', 'email', plus whatever else was added) - any object typed as 'User' must now satisfy the combined shape. If both declarations define the same property name with incompatible types (e.g., one says 'name: string', the other 'name: number'), TypeScript raises a compile error rather than silently picking one, since it can't reconcile them. This mechanism is exactly what powers module augmentation for extending third-party library types (like adding a property to Express's 'Request'), and it's also how TypeScript's own lib declarations let you extend built-in global interfaces such as 'Window' or 'Array'. Note that declaration merging is specific to interfaces (and a few other declaration kinds, like namespaces, classes+namespaces, and enums, each following their own merging rules) - a 'type' alias explicitly cannot be declared twice with the same name; doing so is always a straightforward compile error, which is one of the concrete structural differences between 'interface' and 'type'.

questions.question: What steps would you take to incrementally migrate an existing JavaScript codebase to TypeScript (e.g., `allowJs`, `checkJs`, tightening strictness over time)?
questions.answer: The recommended approach avoids a risky 'big-bang' rewrite in favor of letting TypeScript and JavaScript coexist and migrating gradually. First, add a 'tsconfig.json' with 'allowJs: true', which lets the TypeScript compiler process '.js' files alongside '.ts' files in the same project (without this, importing a '.js' file from a '.ts' file, or vice versa, isn't recognized). Initially leave 'checkJs' off (or 'strict: false') so existing JS files aren't suddenly flooded with type errors before anyone has annotated anything - this lets you introduce the toolchain without breaking the build. Next, convert files incrementally, typically starting from the 'leaves' of the dependency graph (small, low-level utility functions and shared type/model definitions with few dependencies) and working toward higher-level application/UI code, simply renaming '.js' to '.ts' (or '.jsx' to '.tsx') one file or module at a time and fixing whatever type errors surface, using 'any' as a temporary escape hatch where a proper type isn't worth writing yet. For JS files not yet renamed, enabling 'checkJs' plus JSDoc type annotations can get partial type-checking benefit without a full rewrite. Once a meaningful portion of the codebase is converted, progressively tighten compiler strictness - enabling 'noImplicitAny', then 'strictNullChecks', and eventually the full 'strict' family - rather than turning strict mode on all at once, since doing so on a large codebase from day one typically produces an overwhelming number of errors and stalls the migration. Throughout the process, adding CI checks that enforce the current strictness level (and prevent regressions like new 'any' usages) helps keep migration progress from eroding as more people commit code, and tracking metrics like percentage of files converted or count of remaining 'any' usages helps keep the effort visible and on track.

questions.question: How would you properly type a `useState` or `useReducer` hook in a React component, including its associated action types?
questions.answer: For 'useState', TypeScript infers the state's type from the initial value passed in - 'const [count, setCount] = useState(0)' automatically types 'count' as 'number' and 'setCount' as a function accepting a 'number' (or a functional updater). When the initial value doesn't fully capture the type you need (commonly when the state starts as 'null' but will later hold an object, or when a state could be one of several types), you supply an explicit type argument: 'const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);'. For 'useReducer', the recommended pattern is to type both the state shape and, more importantly, the possible actions as a discriminated union, so the reducer function gets exhaustive, precise type-checking in every branch. For example: 'type State = { count: number }; type Action = { type: "increment" } | { type: "decrement" } | { type: "set"; payload: number }; function reducer(state: State, action: Action): State { switch (action.type) { case "increment": return { count: state.count + 1 }; case "set": return { count: action.payload }; ... } }'. Because 'Action' is a discriminated union keyed on the literal 'type' field, TypeScript narrows 'action' to the exact matching variant inside each 'case' - so 'action.payload' is only accessible (and required to exist) inside the '"set"' branch, and referencing it in the '"increment"' branch would be a compile error. This eliminates a whole class of bugs where an action is dispatched with a missing or mistyped payload, and - combined with an exhaustiveness check in the 'default' case - guarantees the compiler flags any new action type you forget to handle in the reducer. 'useReducer<React.Reducer<State, Action>>(reducer, initialState)' (or simply relying on inference from the typed 'reducer' function itself) then correctly types both the returned state and the 'dispatch' function so it only accepts valid 'Action' values.

questions.question: What does the `useUnknownInCatchVariables` compiler option do, and how does it change the type of a variable caught in a `catch` block?
questions.answer: By default (prior to explicitly enabling this option, or on TypeScript versions before 4.4), a variable caught in a 'catch' clause is implicitly typed as 'any' - 'catch (err) { err.message }' compiles fine even though nothing guarantees the thrown value is actually an 'Error' object (in JavaScript, you can 'throw' literally any value: a string, a number, a plain object, etc.). Introduced in TypeScript 4.4, 'useUnknownInCatchVariables' changes that default so the caught variable's type is 'unknown' instead of 'any', forcing you to narrow it (with an 'instanceof Error' check, a custom type guard, or similar) before accessing any properties on it - 'err.message' now becomes a compile error until you've verified the shape at runtime, e.g., 'catch (err) { if (err instanceof Error) { console.log(err.message); } }'. This flag is included as part of the 'strict' family, so enabling 'strict: true' turns it on automatically; it can also be enabled independently for codebases that aren't fully strict yet. It doesn't change JavaScript's runtime behavior at all (you can still throw anything you want) - it only changes what the type checker will let you assume about the caught value without proof, closing a real gap where code often incorrectly assumed every thrown value was an 'Error' instance with a '.message' property. If you specifically want the old, less-safe behavior for a one-off catch block (e.g., quick prototyping code), you can still explicitly annotate 'catch (err: any)', since 'any' and 'unknown' are the only two type annotations TypeScript permits on a catch-clause variable.

questions.question: What is the Result/Either pattern for error handling in TypeScript, and how does returning a `Result<T, E>` compare to using `try`/`catch`?
questions.answer: The Result (or Either) pattern models the outcome of an operation that can fail as an ordinary return value - a discriminated union representing either success (with data) or failure (with an error) - instead of using exceptions and 'try'/'catch' to signal failure out-of-band. A typical definition: 'type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: E };'. A function that might fail returns this union directly rather than throwing: 'async function getUser(id: number): Promise<Result<User, NotFoundError>> { const res = await fetch(...); if (!res.ok) return { ok: false, error: { type: "not_found", id } }; return { ok: true, data: await res.json() }; }'. The caller then handles both branches explicitly: 'const result = await getUser(123); if (result.ok) { console.log(result.data.email); } else { console.log(result.error.type); }' - because 'ok' is the discriminant, TypeScript narrows 'result' to exactly the right variant in each branch, and there's no way to accidentally access 'result.data' without having checked 'result.ok' first. The key advantage over 'try'/'catch' is visibility in the type system: with exceptions, nothing in a function's type signature tells a caller that it might throw, what it might throw, or forces them to handle that possibility - TypeScript's type checker is completely blind to thrown errors, so it's easy to forget a 'try'/'catch' entirely and have an unhandled exception crash the program (or a promise silently reject) at runtime. With 'Result<T, E>', the possibility of failure - and the exact shape of the error - is part of the function's declared return type, so the compiler forces callers to at least acknowledge both branches before using the success value. The trade-off is more verbose call sites (checking 'result.ok' everywhere) and it doesn't eliminate the need for 'try'/'catch' entirely, since truly unexpected runtime exceptions (out-of-memory, a bug in third-party code) still propagate as thrown exceptions regardless of what your own functions return.

questions.question: How would you type a custom iterable object in TypeScript by implementing `Symbol.iterator`?
questions.answer: To make a custom object usable in 'for...of' loops, array/object spread ('[...myObj]'), and destructuring, it needs to implement JavaScript's iterable protocol - an object with a method keyed by the well-known symbol 'Symbol.iterator' that returns an iterator (an object with a '.next()' method returning '{ value, done }' pairs). TypeScript provides built-in generic interfaces - 'Iterable<T>' and 'Iterator<T>' - to type this correctly. A minimal example: 'class Range implements Iterable<number> { constructor(private start: number, private end: number) {} [Symbol.iterator](): Iterator<number> { let current = this.start; const end = this.end; return { next(): IteratorResult<number> { return current < end ? { value: current++, done: false } : { value: undefined, done: true }; } }; } }'. Implementing 'Iterable<number>' on the class both documents the contract and lets TypeScript check that '[Symbol.iterator]' actually returns a conforming iterator; once implemented, 'for (const n of new Range(0, 5)) { ... }' and '[...new Range(0, 5)]' both work and are correctly typed as yielding 'number' values. A common, more concise alternative is to write the method as a generator function using 'function*' and 'yield', since generators automatically satisfy the iterator protocol without manually managing 'done'/'value' state: '[Symbol.iterator](): Iterator<number> { for (let i = this.start; i < this.end; i++) yield i; }' (note this requires the 'downlevelIteration' compiler flag or an ES2015+ 'target' to compile correctly for older JS targets). This underlies how TypeScript types many built-in structures - 'Array<T>', 'Map<K, V>', and 'Set<T>' all implement 'Iterable<T>' (or the appropriate entry-pair type) themselves.

questions.question: What are the pitfalls of using `const enum` in TypeScript, particularly around incompatibility with `isolatedModules` and inlining values across package/module boundaries?
questions.answer: A regular 'enum' compiles to a real runtime JavaScript object; a 'const enum' is meant to be a zero-runtime-cost alternative - the compiler inlines each member's literal value directly at every usage site and, in the ideal case, emits no object for the enum at all, purely for performance/bundle-size reasons. The core pitfall is that this inlining requires the compiler to have full knowledge of the enum's members at the point it processes a file referencing it - which conflicts fundamentally with 'isolatedModules', a widely-used compiler option (required by virtually all modern single-file transpilers like esbuild, SWC, and Babel's TypeScript plugin, which process each file independently without whole-program type information) that guarantees every file can be transpiled in isolation, one at a time. When 'isolatedModules' is on and you import a 'const enum' from a different module (especially an 'ambient' const enum declared in a '.d.ts' file with no accompanying runtime value), TypeScript can't guarantee the inlining will work correctly in a single-file transpilation pipeline, and raises a hard compile error: 'Cannot access ambient const enums when the " - isolatedModules" flag is provided.' This is not a hypothetical edge case - it's caused real, well-documented breakage in production for consumers of major libraries (RxJS, jQuery's type definitions, Fluent UI, next-intl) whenever those libraries exported a 'const enum' from their public API and downstream projects had 'isolatedModules' enabled (which today is essentially the default expectation for any project using webpack+babel, Vite, esbuild, or Next.js). The practical consequence is that publishing a 'const enum' as part of a library's public API is now widely considered an anti-pattern; the common fixes are to use a regular (non-const) 'enum' instead (accepting the small runtime cost), or - increasingly preferred - to skip enums entirely in favor of a union of string literal types or an 'as const' object, both of which have no const-enum-style compilation requirements and work uniformly under any transpilation setup.

questions.question: How would you design a type-safe Redux-like state management system in TypeScript so that action types and their payloads remain in sync?
questions.answer: The core technique - used both in hand-rolled solutions and in Redux Toolkit itself - is to model actions as a discriminated union, typically expressed with a generic 'PayloadAction<Payload, Type extends string = string>' helper: 'type PayloadAction<P, T extends string = string> = { type: T; payload: P };'. You then define each concrete action as an instantiation of that generic with a specific literal 'type' and payload shape (e.g., 'type IncrementAction = PayloadAction<number, "counter/increment">'), and combine all of them into a union representing every action the store can handle: 'type CounterAction = IncrementAction | DecrementAction | ResetAction;'. A reducer typed as '(state: CounterState, action: CounterAction) => CounterState' can then 'switch' on 'action.type', and because 'type' is a literal-typed discriminant, TypeScript narrows 'action' to the exact matching variant inside each case - so referencing 'action.payload' is fully typed to that specific action's payload shape, and it's a compile error to reference a payload field that doesn't exist on the current branch, or to construct/dispatch an action with a 'type' string that isn't part of the union at all (catching typos in action-type strings that plain-JavaScript Redux would only catch at runtime, if ever). To keep the whole store type-safe end-to-end, you'd also type the root state (often via 'ReturnType<typeof rootReducer>' to avoid manually duplicating the shape), and type 'dispatch' so it only accepts values assignable to the combined action union, preventing an entirely unrelated action object from being dispatched by mistake. Real-world Redux Toolkit projects lean on this exact pattern via 'createSlice', which auto-generates correctly-typed action creators and infers the 'PayloadAction<T>' type for each case reducer directly from how you define your reducers, removing most of the manual union-wiring described above while preserving the same underlying type-safety guarantees.

questions.question: How would you approach migrating a very large (e.g., 200,000+ line) JavaScript codebase to TypeScript without freezing feature development, and what trade-offs would you communicate to stakeholders?
questions.answer: At this scale, a full stop-the-world rewrite is essentially never viable - the standard approach is fully incremental adoption running in parallel with normal feature work, so the codebase is in a mixed JS/TS state for an extended period (often many months to a couple of years). Concretely: enable 'allowJs' so TypeScript and JavaScript files coexist and are checked/compiled together from day one; establish a convention that all newly written code (and any file meaningfully touched during regular feature work) is written or converted to TypeScript, rather than dedicating separate 'migration sprints'; and prioritize converting shared, foundational code first - utility functions, core data models, API client/response types - since those unlock stronger typing benefits earlier for everything downstream that consumes them. At very large scale, purely manual, file-by-file conversion becomes a bottleneck, so tooling matters: codemods (e.g., via jscodeshift or tools like 'ts-migrate') can automate a large fraction of the mechanical work (adding parameter/return type annotations from simple inference, converting 'require' to 'import'), and CI enforcement (rejecting new '.js' files, or blocking new 'any' usages) is important to prevent the migration from stalling or backsliding once initial momentum fades - real case studies of migrations at this scale report that skipping CI guardrails leads to fragmented, inconsistent typing conventions across teams (different developers making incompatible ad-hoc typing decisions) that then have to be cleaned up later at extra cost. The trade-offs to communicate to stakeholders are concrete and worth being upfront about: short-term velocity will dip somewhat as engineers pay a learning curve for TypeScript idioms and existing PRs take a bit longer to review/land; there's real risk if strictness is turned on too aggressively too early (a wall of thousands of pre-existing errors that discourages the team and stalls progress, versus gradually tightening 'noImplicitAny' → 'strictNullChecks' → full 'strict' over time); and the payoff - meaningfully fewer production bugs from type mismatches, safer large-scale refactors, and better editor tooling/onboarding - accrues gradually and compounds, rather than delivering an immediate, easily quantified ROI, which is why regularly tracking and sharing concrete migration metrics (percentage of files converted, reduction in 'any' usage, bug counts) is important for keeping stakeholder confidence through a multi-month or multi-year effort.

questions.question: How would you build a generic, type-safe API client (e.g., around `fetch`) so that the response type is inferred from the requested endpoint or a schema?
questions.answer: The foundational technique is a generic wrapper function around 'fetch' where the caller supplies the expected response shape as a type argument, and the function's return type is tied to that argument: 'async function apiCall<T>(url: string, method: HttpMethod = "GET", body?: object): Promise<T> { const res = await fetch(url, { method, headers: {"Content-Type":"application/json"}, body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined }); if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`); return res.json() as Promise<T>; }', used as 'const user = await apiCall<User>("/api/users/1");'. The important caveat is that '.json()' itself returns 'Promise<any>' at the type level - TypeScript has no way to verify at compile time that the JSON returned by the server actually matches 'T', so this pattern gives you convenient inferred types at call sites but not a runtime guarantee; a mismatch between what the server actually sends and what 'T' claims will silently produce incorrectly-typed data rather than an error. A more robust design goes further in one of two directions: (1) Define a single, centralized map of endpoints to their request/response types (e.g., 'type ApiEndpoints = { "GET /users/:id": { response: User }; "POST /users": { body: CreateUserInput; response: User } }') and build a typed client whose method signature is derived from that map via generics and template literal types, so the endpoint string itself drives both the expected request shape and the inferred response type, catching typos in the endpoint path and mismatched request bodies at compile time. (2) Combine generics with runtime schema validation (commonly using a library like Zod) so the response is actually parsed and validated against a schema at runtime, and the TypeScript type is derived from that same schema via 'z.infer<typeof Schema>' - this closes the gap left by a pure generic-inference approach, since a schema mismatch now throws a real runtime validation error instead of silently type-lying. It's also common to model the response as a 'Result<T, E>'-style discriminated union rather than throwing on HTTP errors, so callers are forced to explicitly handle both success and typed error cases.

questions.question: How would you type a higher-order component (HOC) in React + TypeScript so it correctly adds and strips injected props from the wrapped component's prop type?
questions.answer: A HOC is a function that takes a component and returns a new component, and typing it correctly requires generics so the HOC works with any wrapped component's props while (a) requiring that component to accept whatever props the HOC will inject, and (b) removing those injected props from what the wrapped, exported component demands from its own consumers. The pattern: define an interface for the props the HOC injects (e.g., 'interface WithAuthProps { user: AuthUser; logout: () => void }'), then write the HOC as 'function withAuth<T extends object>(WrappedComponent: React.ComponentType<T & WithAuthProps>): React.ComponentType<T> { return function WithAuthComponent(props: T) { const { user, logout, isAuthenticated } = useContext(AuthContext); if (!isAuthenticated) return <LoginForm />; return <WrappedComponent {...props} user={user} logout={logout} />; }; }'. The generic 'T' represents whatever additional 'own' props the wrapped component needs beyond the injected ones; constraining the parameter to 'React.ComponentType<T & WithAuthProps>' ensures you can only pass in a component that actually declares it accepts a 'user' and 'logout' prop (a compile error otherwise, catching a common HOC bug where the wrapped component forgets to destructure an injected prop). The returned component type is 'React.ComponentType<T>' - deliberately not 'T & WithAuthProps' - meaning consumers of the enhanced component only need to supply 'T''s own props; 'user' and 'logout' are fully hidden from the outside since the HOC supplies them internally. A common alternative when the injected props need to be stripped from an already-defined prop type (rather than added via intersection from the start) uses 'Omit<T, keyof WithAuthProps>' to compute the consumer-facing prop type. Edge cases to be aware of: HOCs don't automatically forward 'ref's (you typically need 'React.forwardRef' combined with the generic wrapping to support that), and non-React static properties on the original component (like 'propTypes' or custom statics) aren't automatically hoisted onto the returned component unless you explicitly use a utility like 'hoist-non-react-statics'.

questions.question: Why can TypeScript sometimes narrow a discriminated union incorrectly when one variant's shape is structurally assignable to another's, and how would you restructure the types to avoid it?
questions.answer: TypeScript's narrowing relies fundamentally on structural typing, and discriminated-union narrowing specifically depends on being able to cleanly distinguish variants by a discriminant property's literal type. Problems arise when one union member's shape happens to be structurally assignable to another's - most commonly when a variant's fields are all optional, or when one variant's properties form a strict subset of another's with compatible types - because at certain points in the control flow TypeScript's narrowing algorithm can end up considering a value assignable to (or excluded from) a branch based on general structural compatibility rather than strictly on the discriminant check that was actually performed, producing narrowing results that don't match a developer's intuitive expectation. This is a real, documented class of bugs tracked in TypeScript's own issue tracker (e.g., cases where narrowing a union incorrectly retains or drops a member because it's structurally assignable to another member's shape even after a discriminant-based type guard should have excluded it), and it tends to surface specifically in unions where variants aren't fully 'exclusive' in their structure - for instance, a variant with only optional fields can be structurally compatible with '{}', which can be structurally compatible with almost anything, confusing narrowing logic that isn't purely keyed off a single required literal-typed discriminant. The fix is defensive type design: give every variant in the union a required (not optional) discriminant property with a distinct literal value, avoid unions where one variant's required fields are a strict subset of another's, and prefer marking fields that are truly variant-specific as required-in-that-variant rather than optional-across-all-variants (e.g., instead of '{ type?: "a"; a?: string } | { type?: "b"; b?: string }', which is loosely structured and prone to this issue, use '{ type: "a"; a: string } | { type: "b"; b: string }' with a mandatory discriminant on every branch). When narrowing still misbehaves in an edge case despite well-formed types, an explicit user-defined type guard (a function with an 'x is Type' predicate) that only relies on the discriminant check - rather than TypeScript's automatic control-flow narrowing - gives you full manual control over exactly how narrowing is performed at that call site.

questions.question: How do TypeScript's module resolution strategies (`node`, `node16`/`nodenext`, `bundler`) differ, and how can choosing the wrong one break imports in an ESM project?
questions.answer: 'moduleResolution' controls the algorithm TypeScript uses to turn an import specifier into an actual file on disk, and it needs to match how your code will actually be loaded at runtime (or bundled), or you'll get either false-positive compile errors on imports that would actually work, or, worse, successful compiles that fail at runtime. 'node10' (formerly just 'node') mimics how older CommonJS-only Node.js ('require()') resolved modules before v12 - it predates 'package.json' 'exports'/'imports' fields entirely, so it doesn't understand modern conditional export maps and is now considered legacy; it shouldn't be used for new projects. 'node16'/'nodenext' model the resolution behavior of modern Node.js (v12+), which supports both native ESM ('import') and CommonJS ('require') simultaneously but resolves each differently - these modes read the 'exports'/'imports' fields in a package's 'package.json' and, critically, enforce Node's actual ESM runtime rule that relative import specifiers must include an explicit file extension (e.g., 'import { helper } from "./utils.js"', even though the source file is 'utils.ts' - the '.js' extension is what the file will be named after compilation, and Node's own ESM loader requires it, so TypeScript requires it too, at compile time). Omitting the extension under 'node16'/'nodenext' produces a compile error, and if that check is somehow bypassed, the equivalent omission would produce a genuine runtime 'module not found' error under real Node ESM. 'bundler' (added in TS 5.0) models how modern bundlers like Vite, webpack, and esbuild resolve modules - it also understands package.json 'exports'/'imports' the same as node16/nodenext, but deliberately never requires file extensions on relative imports, since bundlers themselves handle extension resolution and don't literally execute the compiled output the way Node's runtime loader does. The most common real-world breakage: setting 'moduleResolution: "bundler"' in a project whose actual output runs directly under Node.js (no bundler in the loop) - extensionless imports type-check fine but then fail at runtime with a Node.js 'ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND', because 'bundler' mode never enforced the extension requirement that Node's real ESM loader actually needs. The fix is matching the setting to the real runtime target: 'node16'/'nodenext' for code that Node.js executes directly, 'bundler' for code that only ever runs after being processed by a bundler.

questions.question: How would you type a polymorphic React component (e.g., a `Button` that can render `as` a different element or tag) while preserving prop type-safety for whichever element is chosen?
questions.answer: A polymorphic component accepts an 'as' prop letting the consumer choose which underlying HTML tag or component it renders, while still getting fully correct prop typing (autocomplete, required-prop checking) for whatever element they chose. The core building block is React's 'ElementType' type, constrained via a generic: 'type PolymorphicProps<T extends React.ElementType> = { as?: T } & Omit<React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>, "as">;'. Here, the generic 'T' represents the concrete element type (defaulting to something like '"button"' if 'as' isn't provided), 'React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>' pulls in every valid prop for whatever 'T' actually is (so 'href' becomes valid and typed when 'T' is '"a"', 'onClick' is available for interactive elements, etc.), and 'Omit<..., "as">' avoids a naming collision between the injected 'as' prop and any real 'as' prop the underlying element might have. The component itself is then also generic: 'const Button = <T extends React.ElementType = "button">({ as, children, ...rest }: PolymorphicProps<T> & OwnProps) => { const Component = as || "button"; return <Component {...rest}>{children}</Component>; };'. With this setup, '<Button>Click</Button>' renders a real button and only accepts button-valid props; '<Button as="a" href="/x">Link</Button>' is now correctly typed to require/allow 'href' (an anchor-specific prop) and would flag a compile error if you passed 'href' without 'as="a"', or passed 'as="a"' but a prop nonsensical for an anchor. This same technique extends naturally to accepting other React components as the 'as' value (e.g., '<Button as={NextLink} href="/dashboard">'), since 'React.ElementType' covers both intrinsic JSX tags and component types. A common added complexity is properly forwarding refs through a polymorphic component, which typically requires combining this pattern with 'React.forwardRef' and a small amount of extra generic plumbing to keep the ref's type correctly tied to whichever element 'T' resolves to.

questions.question: How would you write a recursive `DeepPartial<T>` utility type that makes all nested object properties optional, including inside arrays and nested objects?
questions.answer: The built-in 'Partial<T>' utility type only makes the top-level properties of 'T' optional - it doesn't reach into nested object properties, so 'Partial<{ user: { name: string; age: number } }>' still requires 'user', if provided, to include both 'name' and 'age' in full. A 'DeepPartial<T>' recursively applies optionality at every level, using a conditional type to branch on what kind of type is currently being processed at each step: 'type DeepPartial<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? DeepPartial<U>[] : T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> } : T;'. Walking through the branches: if 'T' is an array, it recurses into the array's element type 'U' (extracted via 'infer') and wraps the result back in an array, so arrays of objects also get their nested properties made optional rather than the array itself being treated as an opaque leaf; if 'T' is some other kind of object, it maps over every key with '?:' (making the property itself optional) and recursively applies 'DeepPartial' to each property's value type, so nested objects keep getting the same treatment at every depth; if 'T' is neither an array nor an object (a primitive like 'string', 'number', a function, etc.), the recursion bottoms out and 'T' is returned unchanged, since there's nothing further to make 'partial'. Applied to 'interface User { name: string; address: { street: string; city: string } }', 'DeepPartial<User>' allows '{ address: { city: "NYC" } }' to type-check, with every field at every level optional. This is the same general recursive-mapped-type technique used to implement other deep utility types like 'DeepReadonly<T>' - the difference is only in which modifier ('?' vs 'readonly') is applied at each mapped level. A practical caveat: this naive version treats special built-in types like 'Date', 'Map', or class instances as plain objects too, recursively (and often incorrectly) mapping over their properties, so production-grade versions typically special-case such types to be left as-is rather than recursed into.

questions.question: How would you write compile-time type tests for a utility type (e.g., using `tsd`, `expect-type`, or a custom `Equal`/`Expect` helper) to verify it behaves correctly across edge cases?
questions.answer: Type-level tests verify that a generic or utility type produces the exact expected type for a range of inputs, catching regressions that ordinary unit tests (which only check runtime values) can't - a utility type can be 'runtime correct' in the sense that nothing throws, while still silently inferring the wrong type, and only a type-level assertion catches that. There are a few common approaches. A minimal hand-rolled version uses a pair of conditional-type helpers: 'type Equal<X, Y> = (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false; type Expect<T extends true> = T;' - the deliberately convoluted 'Equal' definition (comparing two generic conditional types rather than a simple 'X extends Y ? Y extends X ? true : false : false') is intentional, since a naive mutual-extends check can incorrectly report 'true' for certain distinct-but-mutually-assignable types (like 'any' vs a concrete type); this 'distributive-conditional-in-a-function-position' trick avoids that pitfall. You then write assertions like 'type test1 = Expect<Equal<DeepPartial<User>, ExpectedType>>;' directly in a '.ts' file - if the types don't match exactly, 'Expect' fails to compile (a red squiggly in the editor and a 'tsc' error), giving you a compile-time-only test with zero runtime cost, run simply by including that file in your normal 'tsc' build or a dedicated type-check script. For a more full-featured setup, the 'tsd' package lets you write '.test-d.ts' files using an 'expectType<T>(value)' / 'expectError()' API and runs them via a CLI that specifically checks the type output rather than executing the code, commonly used by library authors to guard a package's public '.d.ts' API against regressions; similarly, the 'expect-type' package offers a fluent, zero-runtime-overhead API (e.g., 'expectTypeOf<DeepPartial<User>>().toEqualTypeOf<ExpectedType>()') that integrates naturally alongside existing test files without needing a separate test runner. In practice, all these approaches are used specifically for testing complex, reusable utility types (conditional types, mapped types, generic constraints) shipped as part of a library's public API, where a subtle unintended change in inferred output would otherwise only be caught much later by downstream consumers hitting confusing type errors.
